doc.title: Josiah Gluck interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 13, 2022

title: Recording orchestras with few microphones and the Decca Tree
summary: Orchestras are best recorded with minimal mics such as the Decca Tree, so balance is the conductor's job, unlike film scoring.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I had this — I was listening to a symphony, a Beethoven symphony the other day and the balance of the instrumentation. I wonder if you’ve had the experience of recording an orchestra and then sitting with the conductor who has been responsible for the sound of the orchestra but now he wants to hear more violas. Is that even possible in that setting?

It can be, depending on what kind of forest of microphones you have put up, but typically orchestras should be recorded with as few microphones as possible. Film score recording has a much bigger forest of microphones because you may want to pick things out to help you in and around dialogue and exploding planets and spaceships or what have you. But if something is done in a very bare bones, traditional manner, what they call the Decca Tree with three microphones hung in front of the orchestra and then maybe a couple of

outriggers further out. “You want more violas, Maestro? Might I suggest at bar whatever they dig in a little more. Because this microphone array is designed to pick up where all the sound is coming to one spot. Typically it’s like a tripod of mics up above the conductor. I think it’s supposed to be like 10-1/2 feet above his head or something like that, and all the sound is arriving there which is how you want to experience that. So if he wants to hear more he’s got to dig in or she has to tell them, “Moose call, ocarina, zither at bar 75, play louder.”
You must like ocarinas, that’s the second time that’s come up.
